summary: This standards-track document defines a unicast-based way to speed up joining a multicast RTP session. A joining receiver may wait for reference information; the unicast burst provides it so playback starts sooner.

eli5.summary: Joining a live show mid-way, you wait for a good moment to start. A helper quickly sends what you missed.

questions: how to join multicast video faster
what is rams rapid acquisition of multicast rtp sessions
how to speed up iptv channel change
subtitle: How a receiver joining a multicast RTP stream gets a fast unicast head start instead of waiting for the next key information.

tldr.problem: A receiver joining a multicast session at a random moment must wait for Reference Information before it can use the data, which makes switching channels slow.
tldr.mechanism: Before joining, the receiver asks a retransmission server over RTCP for a unicast burst of cached packets sent faster than the normal rate, then joins the multicast once the burst has caught up.
tldr.outcome: The method defines three RTCP messages (request, information, termination), SDP signaling and registries. It is meant for managed edge networks, not for use across best-effort Internet paths.

today: RFC 6285 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text limits its use to networks where bottlenecks are known, not best-effort Internet paths.

sections.title: The Idea: A Unicast Head Start
sections.content:
Many multicast flows need Reference Information before any data can be used: a schema, references to which data to process, encryption information and so on. It is normally repeated periodically in the session. A receiver that joins just after it was sent has to wait for it to come around again. The RFC calls the time from wanting to join until all the Reference Information has arrived the Acquisition Delay.

The method, called Rapid Acquisition of Multicast RTP Sessions (RAMS), addresses source-specific multicast sessions. A Retransmission Server joins the multicast session, caches the Reference Information and acts as a feedback target. A joining receiver first sends it a request, receives the Reference Information over a new unicast RTP session, and may get it faster than the natural rate if bandwidth is spare. Once it has what it needs, it joins the multicast session. The main use case named is cutting channel-change times in IPTV networks.

The design deliberately reuses existing RTP and RTCP tools: the unicast retransmission support of RFC 4588 and RTCP feedback from RFC 4585. There are always two RTP sessions in one run of the protocol: the primary multicast session with its unicast feedback, and the unicast burst session.
sections.eli5: Instead of waiting for the next time the TV station repeats its important info, you ask a helper nearby to send it to you right now, quickly.

sections.title: Where the Delay Comes From
sections.content:
The RFC splits acquisition delay into three parts.

  • Multicast-switching delay: leaving the old session and joining the new one through a group management protocol such as IGMP version 3 or MLD version 2. The RFC says current systems usually have join latencies below 200 ms, though lost Join or Leave messages add more.
  • Reference Information latency: how long until the receiver has the information. It is small for flows with little interdependency and can be large for compressed audio and video.
  • Buffering delays: loss repair such as forward error correction and retransmission needs buffers, de-jittering adds more, and video decoders may need up to a few seconds of coded data before starting.
sections.eli5: Switching channels is slow for three reasons: knocking on the new channel's door, waiting for the key info, and filling up a waiting cup before playing.

sections.title: Design Constraints
sections.content:
Rapid acquisition is an optimization, so the system must keep working if it fails. A failed attempt must not leave the user worse off than simply joining, and it must not damage the multicast session being joined or other traffic sharing the network.

The RFC explains why usual tools do not fit. Bursts are high-rate and short, so per-flow admission control such as RSVP has too much latency, and a TCP-like handshake and slow start would add many round trips and defeat the purpose. Instead the goals are a deterministic upper bound on the extra bandwidth (a reasonable bound is e*B, where B is the nominal multicast bandwidth and e is an excess-bandwidth coefficient), minimal overlap between burst and multicast, and minimal gap between them.

The RFC says the solution assumes the server and receivers know where the bottleneck is, which generally holds only in the same edge network. It should not be used across any best-effort path of the Internet.
sections.eli5: The quick recap has to be speedy but not hog the road, and if it fails you should still be able to just watch the live show.

sections.title: How a Rapid Acquisition Runs
sections.content:
The server side has two logical parts that the RFC treats as one Retransmission Server: the Feedback Target (FT) and the Burst/Retransmission Source (BRS). The receiver is called RTP_Rx. The steps are:

  • Port mapping setup: the receiver tells the FT which ports it will use for the unicast session, using the method of RFC 6284.
  • Request: the receiver sends a RAMS Request (RAMS-R) to the feedback target, optionally limiting buffer and bandwidth.
  • Response: the BRS answers with RAMS Information (RAMS-I) messages, accepting or rejecting. Rejection of the whole session uses code 510, and the receiver can then just join the multicast.
  • Unicast burst: accepted streams are sent as RTP retransmission packets in a separate unicast session.
  • Join signaling: RAMS-I tells the receiver when it may send the group management Join. Joining too early risks loss from overlap; too late leaves a gap that NACK retransmission requests can fill.
  • Terminate: by default the receiver sends a RAMS Termination (RAMS-T) after it joins, carrying the sequence number of the first multicast packet it received. The BRS stops after the burst packet just before that number. An RTCP BYE ends everything.

Normally RTCP feedback cannot be sent for a minimum of one second after joining (Tmin of 1.0 second). This method initializes Tmin to zero so the first request can go out immediately.

If messages are lost, the receiver may resend its request under the RTCP timer rules or time out and simply join. The RFC recommends repeating RAMS-I and RAMS-T messages for redundancy, and requires the BRS to stop bursting when it can no longer send faster than the multicast arrives.
sections.eli5: You ask the helper for a recap, the helper sends it fast and tells you when to switch to live, and you tell the helper to stop once you are watching live.

sections.title: Burst Shaping and Congestion
sections.content:
A faster burst gets the receiver started sooner and means the server sends less overall, since the burst runs until it catches up with the multicast. But a faster burst raises the risk of congestion loss, so there must be an upper bound.

The BRS can use the receiver's stated limits, RTCP receiver reports from the unicast session, NACKs, ECN markings, updated requests, transport feedback such as DCCP ACKs, or preconfigured limits. Where the bottleneck is known and provisioned, such as a managed IPTV network, the BRS MUST start above the nominal rate but within the engineered limit. Where it cannot find a reliable value, it should start no higher than the nominal bitrate and increase gradually. In both cases it MUST keep monitoring for congestion loss, and the receiver should send a report at least once every two round-trip times.

If congestion persists, the BRS ends the burst with a RAMS-I carrying a response code, and the receiver decides when to join. Near the end of the burst, burst and multicast packets may briefly overlap, so the BRS can lower the burst rate as the join approaches.
sections.eli5: The recap can be sent fast, but if the road gets jammed the helper slows down or stops, and you just switch to live.

sections.title: The RAMS Messages
sections.content:
RAMS messages are RTCP transport-layer feedback messages using the common format of RFC 4585, with packet type RTPFB (205) and FMT value RAMS (6). A one-octet sub-feedback message type (SFMT) tells them apart: 1 for the request, 2 for information, 3 for termination.

Optional fields are TLV elements: a one-octet Type, a reserved octet, a two-octet Length and a Value, padded to a 32-bit boundary. Unknown vendor-neutral or private extensions MUST be ignored. Types 128 to 254 are reserved for private extensions, which carry an Enterprise Number.

  • RAMS-R carries the Requested Media Sender SSRC(s) (type 1; a Length of zero asks for the whole session), Min and Max RAMS Buffer Fill (types 2 and 3, in milliseconds), Max Receive Bitrate (type 4), Preamble-only Allowed (type 5) and Supported Enterprise Numbers (type 6).
  • RAMS-I carries an 8-bit message sequence number, a 16-bit response code and TLVs such as the first packet sequence number (type 32), Earliest Multicast Join Time in ms (type 33), Burst Duration (type 34) and Max Transmit Bitrate (type 35).
  • RAMS-T optionally carries the extended RTP sequence number of the first multicast packet (type 61).

Response codes follow HTTP-style levels: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 4xx receiver errors, 5xx server errors.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of notes: one asks for the recap, one describes it and says when to switch, and one says you are done.

sections.title: SDP Signaling and NAT
sections.content:
Support is advertised declaratively in SDP. The RFC adds the value rai (Rapid Acquisition Indication) to the nack feedback type of rtcp-fb, and a media-level attribute rams-updates that says the server accepts updated requests. Without it the receiver SHALL NOT send updated requests, though it may repeat its initial request unchanged. The text requires related support, among it RTP/AVPF, the RTP retransmission payload format, unicast RTCP feedback for SSM sessions, RTP and RTCP multiplexing on the unicast session and the port-mapping attribute.

To request only some streams, the receiver must learn their SSRCs (and CNAME) from the ssrc attribute in the SDP. For a single stream or a whole session this is not needed. With rapid acquisition on, the rtx-time parameter means how long in milliseconds the BRS keeps a packet cached.

For NAT, a NAT must see traffic from the receiver to the server first, or be configured to forward ports. In the first case the receiver MUST send UDP traffic at least every 30 seconds to keep the binding alive. Applications using RAMS MUST support the port-mapping method of RFC 6284 on both sides.
sections.eli5: The call setup note says whether the helper exists. If your home router is in the way, you must nudge it regularly so it lets the helper's messages through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because bursts run faster than the nominal rate, RAMS can make denial-of-service attacks more harmful than ordinary retransmission. Tampered or spoofed RAMS-R messages can start inappropriate bursts or change a running one, for example by altering Max Receive Bitrate. Tampered RAMS-T can cut a burst short, and tampered RAMS-I can mislead the receiver. RAMS-R and RAMS-T have no replay protection, while RAMS-I has a sequence number that makes replay less likely.

Mitigations in the text: protect SDP integrity, validate source addresses, use SRTP and SRTCP, and have receivers and the server perform a DTLS-SRTP handshake over the RTCP channel. The server should also reject unreasonable values, such as a Min Buffer Fill of many seconds, and police per endpoint. The receiver should treat a join time far in the future, with no burst arriving, as a possible man-in-the-middle sign. A subverted retransmission server is almost impossible to protect against.
sections.eli5: A fast recap service can be abused to flood someone, so the messages should be protected and the helper should say no to silly requests.
